CABER?  ABIE? INDIANA HOOSIER and BOOLEAN ALGEBRA as clued?  This is not a Wednesday puzzle.

Also, there are a lot of partials and abbreviations, some of which, like ODU, shouldn't have made it to print.  We've also got TNN, PHD, ADM, ESE, CENO, NNE, TBS, and RNA.

I had moe (mow) for the groundskeeper name, which threw off the bottom right for a while. I didn't know ABIE either, so the bottom word was eOS_S for quite a while. Then I deleted moe and put ALGEBRA in, which left me with a very confused _OS_S and LO_. (Log? Low? Neither are names.  Lol? Loo?)

I tried to make the two-part answers have a connected meaning. Failing that, it was mix and match time:

BOOLEAN MASSAGES:  you can request feet and neck, or feet or neck, or not feet and not neck.

CARBON ICED TEA: specialty of backyard charcoal barbecue.

WESTERN NOWHERE: municipality not far from Nowhere Junction and Center Nowhere.
Great change for a Wednesday. Clever and varied clues.

Interesting Wednesday today with every across being two word.  Usually I do a few rows of across, a few rows of down, a few more rows of across, etc but today I did all the downs first.

A few interesting traps in today's puzzle.  First the fact yesterday had "Actress Polo" and answer TERI and today had "Actress Teri" but the answer was not POLO was really sneaky.

Then in southeast corner, first I had COUNTS HEADS.  Then I took off HEADS because I thought the groundskeeper name was MOE.  And turns out it was NOSES and LON?  Also a bit sneaky, both make sense but less sense than something else that fits in the same space.

HEAD MASSAGER was also a tough one to think of as first I was wondering what could take place in an actual temple.

Clever puzzle, just a few sneaky tricks.

I was a touch disappointed that the down clues didn’t put up much of a fight after all, but that also meant I got to enjoy the lively fill while keeping my older son company as he fell asleep, so it’s all good.

What a beautiful FEAT of construction, Mr. Bodily. Thank you for your dedication and persistence in creating this grid. It made for a nice change of pace, being so dependent on the downs to crack open the acrosses. Even knowing that would be the case, our brilliant constructor didn't let us off the hook too easy. Case in point: city on the Guanabara Bay. Yes, you all know that I know it, but that doesn't mean I empathize any less with those who don't. In fact, my thought was "How are people supposed to know that? It's so specific, not run-of-the-mill such as referencing Ipanema, or Copacabana, or Sugar Loaf Mountain, or the Christ The Redeemer statue." Normally, we could say "get it from the crosses" but, in this case, we were trying to get the crosses! I ran into that problem with TNN, CENO, ODU, and CABER – which forced me to think and maneuver around them, and I loved it! (Here is a fun video that promoted Rio for the 2016 Olympics, to the tune of the official anthem of the city of Rio de Janeiro: https://youtu.be/30HM-O9LajQ?is=K6307Z6qZJj2a47G And here is the city's anthem as sung by Caetano Veloso, a legend of Brazilian Pop Music, with a Bossa Nova twist: https://youtu.be/GCJVGtQswOw?is=9_MizTwpV8JPP8Tq) Thanks again. Mr. Bodily. You never cease to amaze me!

Okay, regarding the difficulty of making this puzzle, I’ll just say this.  It took Joel Fagliano, a pro’s pro constructor, five years to make a similar one (7/30/2020), and from his notes, it sounds like most of the time was spent pulling out his hair.

Two points:

First, every across answer today not only has its crossing answers to aid in solving, but another across answer as well!  That was a new solving experience, and just felt very cool and quite wonderful.  

Second, 11 of the 14 paired answers are NYT debut answers!  What?  Really?  Read those phrases, they all sound in the language.  Daniel somehow filled this seemingly impossible-to-make puzzle with remarkable freshness!

That first point made the outing fun and memorable.  The second, well, the skill that underpinned the making of this blew me away.  

Daniel, sir, part of me is bowing down, and part of me is pumping my fists in a raving standing-O.  This was a gem.  Thank you!

Today is their moment in the spotlight:  an homage to Down seems overdue, and Mr. Bodily has done them proud.

Y’all have a lovely day, be kind, and celebrate the Down clues wherever you find them.

In re Pronunciation/regional differences, etc.

I get asked where DHubby and I "are from."  If I say I am a Georgia native, I get, "You certainly don't sound like you're from the South."  DHubby, a Pennsylvanian, doesn't seem to have any regional accent either.  
In part, I had to work to differentiate some vowel sounds (think pin/pen) to better serve my Adult Basic Reading students.  
There was also a hurdle in that Phonics were NOT a part of my early education.  (The "Look-Say" Method--dick, jane, baby sally--did a disservice to millions of young students.  Lucky kids kind of figured out the sound/symbol system, but usually imperfectly.)  I took Phonetics my senior yr of college, discovered Flesch's _Why Johnny Can't Read_, and (I hope) helped many students find their way out of the dark.  But there are still anti-phonics people out there.....

I am convinced that this puzzle called upon an entirely different part of my brain than I use to solve other crosswords.  Familiar guideposts were scuttled and I realized that I wasn't going to have any help from crosses -- at least not for a while.  Which might have been OK if there hadn't been so many names in the Downs. But we crossword solvers are spoiled: we expect the Acrosses and Downs to help each other out -- and usually they do.

Interestingly, I was watching something online yesterday that talked about how perfecting something you already do doesn't help protect the brain from the ravages of aging.  You need to challenge it with something entirely different:  Learn a new language.  Learn to play a musical instrument.  Question:  If I do enough puzzles like this one, can I avoid learning a new language or playing an instrument?

Eventually I cracked this, with the exception of two answers.  1) Was it HARD CASE/HABER or CARD CASE/CABER?  I guessed wrong.  And 2) Was it BODLEAN/DDU or BOLLEAN/LDU?  I never thought of BOOLEAN.  That's on me; an educated person should know BOOLEAN, right?   But I thought BODLEAN rang a bell.  And you know what I think of "sch" initialisms, which is unprintable in a family newspaper.

Did I have fun with this and find it challenging?  Actually I found it fairly painful -- but I suppose that's on me, too.
